How it works

# How Bedrock Roof works
A free, simple way to get a roofer out to look at your roof. Here's exactly what happens, and how we're paid.

## 1. You send a request
Choose what you need (new roof, repair, storm damage or inspection) and enter your name, mobile number and ZIP code. A short note helps the roofer come prepared.

## 2. We match you with a local roofer
We pass your request to an independent roofing contractor that serves your ZIP code. We aim to send each request to one roofer so your phone doesn't ring off the hook. If we can't find anyone in your area, we'll let you know.

## 3. The roofer contacts you
The roofer calls or texts to set up a free inspection. They'll look at the roof, answer your questions and give you a written quote.

## 4. You decide
There's no obligation. Compare the quote with others, check the contractor's license and insurance (here's how) and hire only if it's right for you. Any contract is between you and the roofer.

## How we make money
Bedrock Roof is free for homeowners. Roofing contractors may pay us a fee for introductions to homeowners who asked to be contacted. That fee never gets added to your bill by us, and it doesn't change your right to say no.

## What we are not
We are not a roofing contractor and we don't perform, inspect, guarantee or warranty roofing work. We don't handle insurance claims and can't promise any claim will be approved. Roofers are independent businesses, so always verify a roofer's license and insurance yourself before signing.

Homeowner guide

# How much does a roof replacement cost?
Here are typical national price ranges, the factors that move the number up or down, and how to compare quotes so you're not overpaying.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: A full roof replacement in the U.S. averages about $9,500, and most jobs fall between about $5,800 and $46,000. That works out to roughly $4 to $11 per square foot. Source: Angi data, as reported by NerdWallet.

These are national ballpark figures. Your price depends on your roof and your market, and the only way to know for sure is a written quote after an inspection.

## What drives the cost

- Roof size. Roofers price by the "square" (100 sq ft of roof). Your roof area is usually larger than your home's floor area.

- Material. Asphalt shingles are the most affordable. Metal, wood shakes, clay or concrete tile and slate cost more but can last longer.

- Pitch and complexity. Steep roofs, multiple levels, chimneys, skylights and valleys take more labor. NerdWallet notes steep pitches can add roughly $1,000 to $3,000.

- Tear-off and repairs. Removing old layers and replacing rotted decking adds cost. Ask how decking repairs are priced before you sign.

- Labor and location. Labor is often more than half the bill and is higher in high-cost areas and after big storms.

- Permits and warranty. Many areas require a permit. Extended manufacturer warranties are optional extras.

## Common roofing materials

Material | Cost | Good to know | 

Asphalt shingle | $ | Most common in the U.S. and the most budget-friendly. | 

Metal | $$ | Long-lasting and sheds snow and rain well. Costs more up front. | 

Wood shake | $$ | Natural look. Needs more upkeep and may face fire-code limits. | 

Clay or concrete tile | $$$ | Popular in warm climates. Heavy, so the structure must support it. | 

Slate | $$$$ | Premium and very long-lived. Needs a specialist installer. | 

## How to compare quotes

- Get at least two or three written quotes for a full replacement.

- Make sure each one covers the same scope: tear-off, underlayment, flashing, vents, drip edge, cleanup and disposal.

- Ask how decking replacement is priced (per sheet is common).

- Compare warranties: the manufacturer's warranty on materials and the contractor's warranty on workmanship.

- Be wary of a quote far below the others. It may leave things out.

## Can insurance pay for it?
Homeowners insurance may cover damage from a sudden event like hail or wind, but usually not wear and tear from age. Coverage depends on your policy and your insurer's decision. A roofer can document damage, but no one can promise approval. See what to do after storm damage.

## Related guides
Roofing materials comparedMetal roof vs. asphalt shingles: which is better?What to expect during a roof replacementDoes insurance cover roof replacement?

## Frequently asked questions

### What's the average cost to replace a roof?
Angi's figures, as reported by NerdWallet, put the national average around $9,500, with most jobs between about $5,800 and $46,000 depending on size, material and location.

### How much does a roof cost per square foot?
About $4 to $11 per square foot for a typical replacement, according to Angi data cited by NerdWallet. Premium materials like slate and clay tile cost more.

### Why are my quotes so different?
Quotes vary with the materials, how many layers come off, whether decking needs replacing, ventilation and flashing work, the warranty offered, and the contractor's overhead. Ask each roofer to itemize so you compare the same scope.

Homeowner guide

# How to choose a roofer you can trust
A roof is one of the biggest repairs most homeowners ever pay for. Use this checklist before you sign with anyone, including any roofer you meet through us.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

## Before you hire: the checklist

- Check the license. Look the company up on your state contractor licensing board, or your city or county if your state doesn't license roofers. Make sure the name matches the contract.

- Ask for proof of insurance. Ask for certificates of general liability and workers' compensation insurance, and call the insurer to confirm they're current.

- Look for a local address and track record. A real business address, reviews on independent sites and references from recent jobs near you.

- Get it in writing. A detailed written estimate with materials, scope, cleanup, timeline, permit and payment schedule.

- Understand the warranty. Ask about both the manufacturer's material warranty and the contractor's workmanship warranty, and get both in writing.

- Confirm the permit. Ask who pulls the permit. In most places it should be the contractor.

- Pay sensibly. Avoid paying most of the cost up front or in cash. Pay by check or card so there's a record.

## Red flags

- Knocking on doors right after a storm and pressing you to sign that day.

- Offering to "cover" or waive your insurance deductible. That can be insurance fraud in many states.

- No license number, no written estimate, or a contract with blanks in it.

- Asking you to sign over insurance benefits before you understand what you're agreeing to.

- A price far below every other quote.

## 7 questions to ask any roofer

- What's your license number, and can I see your insurance certificates?
- Will you pull the permit?
- Who will be on the roof: your crew or subcontractors?
- What exactly does the quote include, and how is rotted decking priced?
- What warranties do I get, and who backs them?
- How long will the job take and how do you protect my yard and gutters?
- Can I talk to two customers whose roofs you did this year?

Roofers we connect you with are independent businesses. We encourage you to run every one through this checklist.

## Related guides
Roofing scams and red flagsRoof warranties explainedDo you need a permit to replace your roof?How much does a roof replacement cost?

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I check a roofer's license?
Search your state's contractor licensing board website using the company's name or license number. Licensing rules vary by state, and in some states roofers are licensed by the city or county instead.

### Should I pay a deposit up front?
A reasonable deposit for materials is common, but be cautious with anyone who wants most or all of the money before work starts, or wants cash only. Check whether your state limits deposits.

### How many quotes should I get?
For a full replacement, two or three written quotes covering the same scope is a good rule of thumb.

Homeowner guide

# What to do after storm damage to your roof
Hail, high wind or a hurricane can damage a roof in minutes. Here's what to do in the hours and days after, in the right order.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

## 1. Stay safe
Don't climb on a wet or damaged roof. Watch for downed power lines, and if water is coming through a ceiling near lights or outlets, turn off power to that area if it's safe to do so.

## 2. Document everything
Take dated photos and video of the roof from the ground, damaged shingles in the yard, gutters, siding, windows and any leaks or stains inside. Keep receipts for anything you spend.

## 3. Prevent more damage
Your policy may require you to take reasonable steps to prevent further damage, like a tarp over a hole. Put buckets under drips and move belongings. Keep receipts for temporary repairs.

## 4. Call your insurance company
Report the damage and ask about your deductible (some policies have separate wind or hurricane deductibles), what's covered and the next steps. An adjuster may inspect.

## 5. Get a roofer's inspection
A roofer can inspect, document damage with photos and give you a written estimate to share with your insurer. Only your insurance company can decide whether a claim is approved.

## 6. Watch out for storm chasers
After big storms, out-of-town crews often go door to door. Check the license and local address, never pay large sums up front, and don't sign anything under pressure. See our roofer checklist.

## Related guides
How to file a roof insurance claim, step by stepHow to tell if hail damaged your roofRoofing scams and red flagsRoof leaking? What to do right now

## Frequently asked questions

### Will insurance cover storm damage to my roof?
It may, if your policy covers the type of damage (for example wind or hail) and the damage came from a covered event rather than age or wear. Your insurer decides. Read your policy and talk to your agent.

### How soon should I file a claim?
Report damage to your insurer promptly. Many policies set deadlines for reporting, so check yours.

### Should I sign with the first roofer who knocks?
Take your time. Get a written estimate, check the license and insurance, and get more than one opinion before signing.

# How to tell if hail damaged your roof
Hail damage is easy to miss from the ground. Here are the signs to look for after a storm and what to do next.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

## Signs to look for from the ground

- Dents in gutters, downspouts, vents and air-conditioning units.
- Granules from shingles collecting in gutters or at the bottom of downspouts.
- Damaged siding, window screens or outdoor furniture.
- Shingle pieces in the yard.

## What hail does to shingles
Hail can leave dark spots where granules were knocked off, soft "bruises" that feel like a bruised apple, and cracks or punctures. Damage that looks minor can still shorten a roof's life. Please don't climb on the roof yourself. A roofer can inspect safely and photograph what they find.

## After a hailstorm

- Photograph damage you can see from the ground, along with the hail itself if you can, with dates.
- Get a roofer's inspection and written findings.
- Report the damage to your insurer and ask about your deductible. Some states and policies have separate wind and hail deductibles.
- Be careful with storm chasers knocking on doors. Check the license and local address of anyone you hire. See how to choose a roofer.

## Related guides
Are Class 4 impact-resistant shingles worth it?How to file a roof insurance claim, step by stepWhat to do after storm damageRoofing scams and red flags

## Frequently asked questions

### Can hail damage a roof without causing a leak?
Yes. Hail can bruise shingles and knock off the protective granules, which shortens the roof's life and can lead to leaks later.

### How long do I have to file a hail claim?
It depends on your policy and state. Many policies set a deadline for reporting damage, so check yours and report promptly.

### What are impact-resistant shingles?
Shingles tested to resist hail impacts, often labeled Class 4. They cost more, but some insurers in hail-prone states offer premium discounts for them.

Homeowner guide

# Roof leaking? What to do right now
A drip from the ceiling is stressful. Here's how to limit the damage today and get the leak fixed for good.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

## Right now: limit the damage

- Move furniture and electronics out of the way and put a bucket under the drip.
- If a ceiling stain is bulging, water may be pooling above it. Carefully poke a small hole in the center to let it drain into a bucket, which can keep the ceiling from collapsing.
- If water is near light fixtures or outlets, turn off power to that area at the breaker if you can do so safely.
- Take photos and video of the leak and any damage.

## Common causes of roof leaks

- Flashing around chimneys, vents, skylights and walls that has cracked, rusted or pulled away.
- Missing or damaged shingles after wind or hail.
- Pipe boots (the rubber seals around plumbing vents) that have cracked with age.
- Ice dams in cold climates that push water under shingles.
- Clogged gutters that back water up under the roof edge.
- An aging roof where the shingles and underlayment have simply worn out.

## Get it inspected
Water often travels along rafters before it drips, so the leak on your ceiling may be several feet from the hole in the roof. A roofer can trace it and tell you whether a repair will do or whether the roof is near the end of its life. See repair or replace?

## Related guides
Should you repair or replace your roof?What to do after storm damage9 signs you might need a new roofHow to file a roof insurance claim, step by step

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I put a tarp on my roof myself?
Only if it's safe. Wet and steep roofs are dangerous. Many roofers offer emergency tarping, and your insurer may expect reasonable steps to prevent more damage.

### Will homeowners insurance pay for a roof leak?
It depends on the cause. Sudden damage, like a tree limb or wind, is often covered, while leaks from age or wear usually aren't. Your policy and insurer decide.

Homeowner guide

# Does homeowners insurance cover roof replacement?
Insurance can pay for a new roof in some cases, but not all. Here's how it usually works, in plain English.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 This is general information, not insurance or legal advice. Your policy and your insurer decide what's covered.

## What's usually covered
Most standard homeowners policies cover sudden, accidental damage from covered events, such as wind, hail, fire or a falling tree. If a storm damages your roof, your policy may pay to repair or replace it, minus your deductible.

## What usually isn't

- Wear and tear from age.
- Damage from lack of maintenance, like long-term leaks that weren't fixed.
- Problems from poor installation.
- Events your policy excludes, such as flood (which needs separate flood insurance).

## Things that affect your payout

- Your deductible. Some policies, especially in coastal and hail-prone states, have separate percentage deductibles for wind, hail or hurricanes.
- Replacement cost or actual cash value. Actual cash value pays less because it subtracts depreciation for the roof's age.
- Roof age. Some insurers limit coverage on older roofs or ask about roof age before renewing a policy.

## How a roof claim usually works

- Document the damage with dated photos.
- Report it to your insurer promptly.
- An adjuster inspects the roof.
- Get a roofer's written estimate so you can compare it with the adjuster's.
- If you disagree with the decision, ask your insurer how to dispute it.

See also: what to do after storm damage and hail damage.

## Related guides
How to file a roof insurance claim, step by stepWhat to do after storm damageHow to tell if hail damaged your roofRoofing scams and red flags

## Frequently asked questions

### Will insurance replace an old roof?
Usually only if a covered event, like a storm, damaged it. Normal wear and tear from age generally isn't covered. Some policies pay less on older roofs, so read yours.

### What's the difference between replacement cost and actual cash value?
Replacement cost coverage pays to replace the roof with similar materials, minus your deductible. Actual cash value subtracts depreciation for the roof's age, so it pays less.

### Should a roofer handle my insurance claim?
A roofer can document damage and give you an estimate, but your claim is between you and your insurer. Be careful about signing anything that hands over your insurance benefits before you understand it, and never agree to have your deductible waived.

# 9 signs you might need a new roof
Roofs rarely fail all at once. These are the signs roofers look for when deciding whether it's time for a new one.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

- Age. If your roof is approaching the typical lifespan for its material, it's worth an inspection. See how long roofs last.

- Curling or cupping shingles. Edges that turn up or centers that sink are signs of wear or poor ventilation.

- Cracked or missing shingles, especially across several areas of the roof.

- Granules in the gutters. Shingles shed granules as they age, and heavy loss means less protection.

- Daylight in the attic or water stains on rafters and decking.

- Ceiling stains or leaks inside the home.

- A sagging roof line, which can mean water damage or structural problems and should be checked soon.

- Damaged flashing around chimneys, vents and skylights.

- Rising energy bills together with an old roof can point to ventilation or insulation problems.

One sign alone doesn't always mean you need a whole new roof. A good roofer will explain what they see and whether a repair is enough.

## Related guides
What happens during a roof inspection?How long does a roof last?Should you repair or replace your roof?When is the best time of year to replace a roof?

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a roof inspection worth it if I don't see a leak?
Often yes, especially after a big storm or if the roof is getting older. Small problems are cheaper to fix before they become leaks.

### Are black streaks on my roof a problem?
They're usually algae. It's mostly cosmetic, though it can be cleaned, and algae-resistant shingles prevent it.

# How long does a roof last?
Every roof wears out eventually. Here's roughly how long common roofing materials last and what affects their lifespan.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 These are general ranges. Climate, installation quality, ventilation and maintenance can move the real number a lot in either direction.

Material | Typical lifespan | 

Asphalt shingles | Roughly 15 to 30 years, with architectural shingles at the longer end | 

Metal | Often 40 years or more | 

Wood shakes | Roughly 20 to 40 years with upkeep | 

Clay or concrete tile | 50 years or more for the tiles, though the underlayment may need replacing sooner | 

Slate | Often 75 years or more | 

Flat roofs (TPO, EPDM, modified bitumen) | Roughly 15 to 30 years depending on the system | 

## What shortens a roof's life

- Hot, sunny climates and strong UV.
- Hail, wind and storms.
- Poor attic ventilation that traps heat and moisture.
- Overhanging trees, clogged gutters and moss.
- Poor installation.

## How to make it last

- Keep gutters clean and trim back branches.
- Have the roof checked after major storms.
- Fix small problems like loose flashing or cracked pipe boots early.
- Make sure the attic is properly ventilated and insulated.

## Related guides
Roofing materials compared9 signs you might need a new roofHow much does a roof replacement cost?Are Class 4 impact-resistant shingles worth it?

## Frequently asked questions

### What makes a roof wear out faster?
Intense sun and heat, poor attic ventilation, storms, trees rubbing or dropping debris, and poor installation all shorten a roof's life.

### Does a warranty tell me how long my roof will last?
Not exactly. Manufacturer warranties cover material defects and often have conditions. Ask your roofer to explain what's covered and for how long.

# Should you repair or replace your roof?
Not every leak means you need a new roof. Here's how roofers usually think about repair versus replacement.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

## A repair may be enough when

- The damage is limited to a small area, like a few missing shingles or a flashing leak around a chimney or vent.
- The roof is relatively young and otherwise in good shape.
- The decking underneath is solid.

## Replacement makes more sense when

- The roof is near the end of its expected life.
- Shingles are curling, cracking or losing granules across large areas.
- There are multiple leaks, sagging, or soft spots in the decking.
- Repairs keep adding up year after year.
- Your insurer is asking questions about the roof's age or condition.

## Get an honest opinion
Ask the roofer to show you photos of what they found and explain why they recommend repair or replacement. For a big decision, a second opinion is always reasonable.

## Related guides
9 signs you might need a new roofHow much does a roof replacement cost?Roof leaking? What to do right nowHow to choose a roofer you can trust

## Frequently asked questions

### How long does a roof last?
It depends on material, climate, ventilation and installation. Asphalt shingle roofs commonly last a couple of decades, while metal, tile and slate can last much longer.

### Can I put new shingles over old ones?
Some areas allow one layer over another, but many roofers recommend a full tear-off so they can inspect the decking. Local codes may limit layers.

# How to file a roof insurance claim, step by step
A roof claim goes more smoothly when you know the steps and keep good records. Here's the process from storm to final payment.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 This is general information, not insurance or legal advice. Your policy and your insurer decide what's covered.

Quick answer: To file a roof claim, document the damage with dated photos, prevent further damage with a tarp if it's safe, read your policy's deductible and deadlines, report the claim promptly, meet the insurance adjuster with your own roofer if possible, and compare the insurer's estimate to a written roofer's estimate before approving work.

## Step 1: Make sure it's safe, then document everything
Stay off a wet or damaged roof. From the ground, photograph missing shingles, dented gutters and vents, debris and interior water stains. Note the date of the storm. Local news or weather service reports of hail or high winds that day are useful to keep.

## Step 2: Prevent more damage
Most policies expect you to take reasonable steps to stop further damage, like tarping an opening or catching drips. Keep receipts. Your insurer may reimburse reasonable temporary repairs.

## Step 3: Read your policy

- Deductible: Is it a flat amount or a percentage of your home's insured value? Many hurricane and wind-hail deductibles are percentages.
- Roof payment terms: Does the policy pay replacement cost (RCV) or actual cash value (ACV) for the roof? Some policies use a payment schedule based on roof age.
- Deadlines: Note how long you have to report damage and to complete repairs.

## Step 4: Get a professional inspection
A roofer can tell you whether the damage is storm-related and whether repairs are likely to exceed your deductible. Get the findings in writing with photos. Be wary of anyone who pressures you to sign a contract before your claim is decided. See roofing scams and red flags.

## Step 5: File the claim
Report it by phone, app or website. Give the date of loss, describe the damage and share photos. Write down your claim number and the adjuster's name.

## Step 6: The adjuster's inspection
The insurer sends an adjuster to inspect the roof. It often helps to have your roofer there to point out damage. Ask for a copy of the adjuster's estimate.

## Step 7: Compare estimates and resolve differences
Compare the insurer's estimate line by line with your roofer's. Missing items often include drip edge, starter shingles, ice-and-water barrier, permits and code-required upgrades. If something is missing, send documentation and ask for a supplement or re-inspection. If you still disagree, check your policy's appraisal clause or contact your state's department of insurance.

## Step 8: Get the work done and collect the rest
With replacement-cost coverage, insurers often pay the depreciated amount first and release the rest (the "recoverable depreciation") after you send proof the work is complete. Keep the final invoice, permit and photos.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Waiting months to report damage.
- Signing over your claim rights without reading what you signed.
- Accepting an offer to waive your deductible, which is fraud.
- Paying a large deposit before the claim is approved.

Related: does insurance cover roof replacement? and what to do after storm damage.

## Related guides
Does insurance cover roof replacement?What to do after storm damageRoofing scams and red flagsHow to tell if hail damaged your roof

## Frequently asked questions

### Should I call my insurer or a roofer first?
For obvious damage, report it to your insurer promptly, since policies set deadlines. Many homeowners also have a roofer inspect first so they know whether damage is worth a claim, especially when it might be close to the deductible.

### What is the difference between ACV and RCV?
Actual cash value (ACV) pays what the roof was worth at the time of the loss, after depreciation. Replacement cost value (RCV) pays to replace it with a similar new roof, often in two payments: the depreciated amount first and the rest after the work is done.

### What if I disagree with the adjuster?
Ask for the estimate in writing, send your roofer's estimate and photos, and ask for a re-inspection. Many policies include an appraisal clause for disputes over the amount, and you can contact your state's department of insurance.

### Will a roof claim raise my premium?
It can. Insurers price policies using claim history and local risk. A weather claim affecting a whole area is generally treated differently from a one-off claim, but rules vary by state and insurer.

Homeowner guide

# Roofing scams and red flags: how to protect yourself
Most roofers are honest, but storms bring out a few who aren't. These are the scams homeowners run into most, and how to avoid them.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: The biggest roofing red flags are a roofer who knocks on your door right after a storm, pushes you to sign the same day, offers to pay or waive your insurance deductible, wants a large cash payment up front, or can't show a license (where your state requires one) and proof of insurance. Check any roofer before you sign, and never let anyone pressure you into a decision on the spot.

## The most common roofing scams

### 1. The door-knock after a storm
After hail or high winds, crews go door to door offering free inspections. Some are reputable local companies, but some are out-of-town crews that will be gone when the warranty matters. Ask for a local address and look the company up before you let anyone on your roof.

### 2. "We'll cover your deductible"
An offer to pay, rebate or waive your deductible sounds generous, but it means the roofer is either inflating the claim or cutting corners on the work. It's a form of insurance fraud, and states including Texas and Florida specifically prohibit it.

### 3. Damage that wasn't there before
Dishonest inspectors have been caught creating "hail hits" or tearing shingles to make damage look worse. If someone goes up on your roof, ask for clear, dated photos, and consider getting a second opinion before filing a claim.

### 4. The contingency agreement that's really a contract
Some roofers ask you to sign a form "so we can talk to your insurance company." Read it carefully. Some of these forms commit you to hiring that roofer if the claim is approved. Several states regulate these agreements and give you a short window to cancel, so ask what you're signing and get a copy.

### 5. Large cash deposits
Paying most of the job in cash before work starts leaves you with little leverage if the crew never shows up. Pay by check or card, keep receipts, and tie payments to progress, like delivery of materials and completion.

### 6. The too-good-to-be-true price
A bid far below the others can mean skipped underlayment, reused flashing, no permit or uninsured workers. Compare itemized quotes line by line so you know what each one includes.

## Red flags checklist

- Pressure to sign today, or "this price is only good right now".
- No physical local address, or a phone number that goes straight to voicemail.
- Can't or won't show a license (where required) and current certificates of liability and workers' comp insurance.
- Offers to handle your claim "for free" in exchange for a signature.
- Asks you to sign a blank or incomplete contract.
- Won't pull a building permit, or asks you to pull it yourself.
- Only accepts cash.

## How to check a roofer in 10 minutes

- Look up the license or registration on your state or city website. Our state pages explain each state's rules.
- Ask for certificates of insurance and call the insurer to confirm they're current.
- Search the company name with words like "complaint" or "scam", and check your state attorney general's site.
- Ask for two or three local references from the past year.
- Get the warranty, the scope of work and the payment schedule in writing.

## If you think you've been scammed
Stop payment if you can, keep every document and photo, and report it to your state attorney general's consumer protection office and your insurer. The Federal Trade Commission also takes reports at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

For the full hiring checklist, see how to choose a roofer you can trust.

## Related guides
How to choose a roofer you can trustHow to file a roof insurance claim, step by stepWhat to do after storm damageHow much does a roof replacement cost?

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a storm chaser roofer?
A storm chaser is a roofing crew, often from out of state, that follows major hail and wind storms and goes door to door looking for insurance-paid jobs. Some are legitimate, but many are hard to reach once the job is done, which matters when a warranty or leak problem comes up.

### Can a roofer pay or waive my insurance deductible?
No. Your deductible is your share of the claim. Offering to cover or waive it is a form of insurance fraud, and several states, including Texas and Florida, specifically prohibit contractors from offering it.

### Should I sign a contract with a roofer on the day of the inspection?
You don't have to, and it's usually better not to. Get at least two written quotes, check the contractor's license and insurance, and read any contract or insurance agreement before signing.

### How much should a roofing deposit be?
It varies by company and by state, and some states cap deposits on home improvement contracts. Be cautious of anyone who wants a large share of the price in cash before materials arrive, and pay by a traceable method.

Homeowner guide

# Roofing materials compared: asphalt, metal, tile and slate
The right roof depends on your climate, budget, home style and how long you plan to stay. Here's how the main options compare.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: Asphalt shingles are the cheapest and most common choice and typically last 15 to 30 years. Metal costs more but often lasts 40 to 70 years and handles wind, snow and embers well. Concrete and clay tile suit hot, sunny and hurricane-prone areas and can last 50 years or more. Slate lasts the longest but is the most expensive and heaviest.

## Side-by-side comparison
Material | Typical lifespan | Relative cost | Best for | 
Asphalt shingles | 15 to 30 years | $ | Most homes; easy to repair; architectural shingles last longer than 3-tab | 
Impact-resistant (Class 4) shingles | 20 to 30 years | $$ | Hail-prone areas; some insurers offer discounts | 
Standing-seam metal | 40 to 70 years | $$$ | Wind, snow, wildfire areas; long lifespan | 
Metal shingles or panels (exposed fastener) | 30 to 50 years | $$ | Budget metal; fasteners need periodic checks | 
Concrete tile | 50 years or more | $$$ | Hot, sunny and hurricane areas; heavy | 
Clay tile | 50 to 100 years | $$$$ | Spanish and Mediterranean styles; very heavy | 
Natural slate | 75 to 100+ years | $$$$ | Historic homes; needs specialist roofers | 
Wood shakes | 20 to 40 years | $$$ | Look of natural wood; not ideal in wildfire areas unless treated | 
Flat-roof membranes (TPE, EPDM, modified bitumen) | 15 to 30 years | $$ | Low-slope and flat roofs | 

Lifespans are typical ranges and depend heavily on installation quality, ventilation, climate and maintenance. Relative cost compares installed price for a typical home, from $ (lowest) to $$$$ (highest).

## How climate changes the choice

- Hail country (Texas to the Dakotas and the Front Range): impact-resistant shingles or metal. See hail damage.

- Hurricane coasts: high-wind-rated shingles, tile or standing-seam metal installed to local wind codes, plus a sealed roof deck.

- Snow and ice: any good material, plus an ice-and-water barrier at the eaves and proper attic ventilation to prevent ice dams.

- Desert heat: tile or reflective "cool roof" materials to cut heat gain.

- Wildfire areas: Class A fire-rated roofing, such as asphalt, metal or tile, with ember-resistant vents.

- Wet Pacific Northwest: moss-resistant shingles or metal, with careful flashing.

Our city pages list the main roof risks and common material choices for each city.

## Questions to ask about any material

- What wind and impact ratings does this product have, and what does my local code require?
- What does the manufacturer's warranty cover, and does it require a certified installer?
- What underlayment, flashing and ventilation are included in the quote?
- Can my roof structure carry the weight? (Important for tile and slate.)
- Are there HOA or historic-district rules on color or material?

Material is only part of the cost. See roof replacement cost and how long a roof lasts.

## Related guides
Metal roof vs. asphalt shingles: which is better?How long does a roof last?Are Class 4 impact-resistant shingles worth it?How much does a roof replacement cost?

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the most common roofing material in the U.S.?
Asphalt shingles. They cover most American homes because they're affordable, widely available and easy to repair.

### Is a metal roof worth the extra cost?
It can be if you plan to stay in the home a long time. Metal usually costs more up front but often lasts two to three times as long as asphalt shingles and handles wind, snow and wildfire embers well.

### What roof lasts the longest?
Natural slate and clay tile can last a century or more when installed and maintained well. Their weight and cost limit where they're used.

### Can I put a new roof over my old shingles?
Some codes allow one extra layer of asphalt shingles over an existing layer, but many roofers recommend a full tear-off so they can inspect and repair the decking. Your local building code and the shingle manufacturer's warranty terms decide what's allowed.

Homeowner guide

# Are impact-resistant (Class 4) shingles worth it?
If you live where hail is common, Class 4 shingles are worth a close look. Here's what they are and how to decide.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: Impact-resistant shingles carry a Class 4 rating under the UL 2218 test, the highest impact rating for roofing. They usually cost more than standard architectural shingles, but in hail-prone states many insurers offer premium discounts that can offset part of the extra cost over time. They make the most sense in hail country, such as Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska, Colorado and the Dakotas.

## What "Class 4" means
Under UL 2218, steel balls of increasing size are dropped onto the roofing. Class 4 is the top rating: the product showed no cracks after impacts from a ball about 2 inches in diameter. Many Class 4 asphalt shingles use a rubberized (SBS-modified) asphalt that's more flexible than standard shingles. Metal roofing can also earn a Class 4 rating, although it may still dent.

## Pros

- Fewer hail claims and less chance of a full replacement after a moderate hailstorm.
- Possible insurance discounts in hail-prone states.
- Many carry stronger wind ratings too.

## Cons

- Higher up-front cost than standard shingles.
- Not hail-proof. Very large hail can still damage them.
- Discounts vary by insurer and aren't guaranteed.

## How to decide

- Check how often hail hits your area. Our city pages flag hail where it's a main roof risk.
- Ask your insurance agent what discount, if any, applies to a Class 4 roof and what proof they need.
- Get quotes for both standard and Class 4 shingles so you can compare the real price difference.
- Keep the product label or invoice showing the UL 2218 Class 4 rating.

Related: how to tell if hail damaged your roof and roofing materials compared.

## Related guides
How to tell if hail damaged your roofRoofing materials comparedHow to file a roof insurance claim, step by stepHow much does a roof replacement cost?

## Frequently asked questions

### What does Class 4 mean on shingles?
Class 4 is the highest rating in the UL 2218 impact test, in which steel balls are dropped on the shingle. A Class 4 shingle showed no cracking when hit by the largest ball, about 2 inches across.

### Do impact-resistant shingles lower insurance premiums?
Often, in hail-prone states. Many insurers offer a discount for Class 4 roofs, and the size varies widely. Ask your agent before you choose a shingle, and keep the product paperwork.

### Are impact-resistant shingles hail-proof?
No. They resist damage much better than standard shingles, but very large hail can still damage them.

Commercial roofing

# Commercial roofing: free inspections and quotes
For property managers, HOAs, landlords and business owners. Tell us about the building and we'll connect you with an independent commercial roofer.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: Bedrock Roof connects owners and managers of commercial buildings, apartment and condo buildings, HOAs and churches with independent commercial roofing contractors for a free inspection and quote. Most commercial roofs are low-slope systems (TPO, EPDM, PVC, modified bitumen or built-up roofing) or metal, and many can be repaired or restored with a coating instead of fully replaced.

## Who we help

- Property managers handling one building or a portfolio.
- HOAs and condo associations planning repairs or a reserve-funded replacement.
- Apartment and multifamily owners.
- Business owners: retail, restaurants, offices, medical buildings.
- Warehouses and industrial buildings, often with metal or large single-ply roofs.
- Churches, schools and nonprofits.

## Common commercial roof types

- TPO: a white single-ply membrane, widely used on new low-slope roofs. It reflects sunlight and has heat-welded seams.
- EPDM: a black synthetic rubber membrane with a long track record, common in colder climates.
- PVC: a single-ply membrane with heat-welded seams that resists chemicals and grease, which is why it's used on restaurants.
- Modified bitumen: asphalt-based sheets applied in layers, common on smaller flat roofs.
- Built-up roofing (BUR): the traditional "tar and gravel" roof made of alternating layers of bitumen and felt.
- Metal: standing-seam or through-fastened panels, common on warehouses and pre-engineered buildings.
- Roof coatings: silicone, acrylic or polyurethane coatings applied over a sound existing roof to seal it and reflect heat.

See flat roof types compared and commercial roof coatings for details.

## What a commercial inspection usually covers

- The membrane or roof surface, seams and penetrations (HVAC curbs, pipes, vents).
- Drainage: drains, scuppers, gutters and any areas where water ponds.
- Flashing at walls, parapets and edges.
- Signs of trapped moisture in the insulation, sometimes checked with core cuts or an infrared or moisture survey.
- Rooftop equipment and foot-traffic damage.
- The age and warranty status of the roof.

## Before you hire a commercial roofer

- Check the contractor's state license or registration for commercial work. Rules differ by state; see our state pages.
- Ask for certificates of general liability and workers' comp insurance, and to be named as an additional insured if your lease or lender requires it.
- Ask whether the contractor is certified by the membrane manufacturer, which is often required for a manufacturer's system warranty.
- Get a written scope that lists the roof system, insulation, flashing details, warranty terms and how tenants and operations will be protected during the work.
- Ask for references from similar buildings.

## Maintenance matters more on flat roofs
Flat and low-slope roofs don't shed water as quickly as steep roofs, so small problems like a clogged drain or an open seam turn into leaks faster. A twice-yearly inspection and prompt repairs are usually the cheapest way to make a commercial roof last. See our commercial roof maintenance checklist.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does Bedrock Roof help with commercial roofs?
Yes. Owners and managers of commercial buildings, apartment and condo buildings, HOAs, churches, warehouses and retail properties can request a free inspection and quote from an independent commercial roofing contractor.

### What types of commercial roofs are there?
Most commercial buildings have low-slope or flat roofs covered with a single-ply membrane (TPO, EPDM or PVC), modified bitumen or built-up roofing. Metal roofs are common on warehouses and newer buildings. Roof coatings can extend the life of many of these systems.

### How often should a commercial roof be inspected?
Many roofing manufacturers and industry groups recommend an inspection at least twice a year, typically in spring and fall, and after any major storm. Regular inspections are often a condition of keeping a manufacturer's warranty in force.

### Can a commercial roof be restored instead of replaced?
Often, if the existing roof is still mostly dry and sound. A roofer can check for trapped moisture, for example with core samples or an infrared or moisture survey, and tell you whether a coating or restoration system is an option.

### Do commercial roofers need a different license?
It depends on the state. Some states license commercial roofing separately from residential work, or require a general contractor license for commercial jobs. Our state pages explain each state's rules.

Commercial roofing

# Flat roof types compared: TPO, EPDM, PVC and more
Flat and low-slope roofs need different materials than shingled roofs. Here's how the main systems compare.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: The most common flat-roof systems are TPO (white, reflective, heat-welded seams), EPDM (durable rubber, popular in cold climates), PVC (heat-welded and grease-resistant, common on restaurants), modified bitumen and built-up roofing. Most last about 15 to 30 years. Installation quality, drainage and seam details matter as much as the material.

## Side-by-side comparison
System | What it is | Often used for | Typical lifespan | 
TPO | White, reflective; heat-welded seams | Hot climates; most new low-slope roofs | 15 to 30 years | 
EPDM | Black (or white) rubber; glued or taped seams | Cold climates; long track record | 20 to 30+ years | 
PVC | Heat-welded; resists grease and chemicals | Restaurants, chemical exposure | 20 to 30 years | 
Modified bitumen | Asphalt sheets in layers | Small flat roofs, foot traffic | 15 to 25 years | 
Built-up roof (BUR) | Layers of bitumen and felt, often with gravel | Older commercial buildings | 20 to 30 years | 
Coating over existing roof | Silicone, acrylic or polyurethane | Extending a sound existing roof | 10 to 20 years, can be renewed | 

Lifespans are typical ranges and depend on membrane thickness, installation, climate, drainage and maintenance.

## What matters besides the membrane

- Drainage. Tapered insulation, drains and scuppers keep water from ponding.
- Insulation. Replacing a roof is often the time to bring insulation up to the current energy code, which may be required.
- Attachment. Membranes can be mechanically fastened, fully adhered or ballasted. Wind zone and building type drive the choice.
- Edges and flashing. Most flat-roof leaks start at seams, edges, walls and penetrations, not in the middle of the membrane.
- Warranty. Manufacturer warranties vary from material-only to full system coverage and often require a certified installer and regular maintenance.

## Homes with flat roofs
Rowhouses, mid-century modern homes and additions often have flat or low-slope sections. The same materials apply, and shingles should never be used on a roof that's too flat for them.

Related: commercial roofing and roof coatings.

## Related guides
Commercial roofing: free inspections and quotesCommercial roof coatings: restore or replace?Roofing materials comparedCommercial roof maintenance checklist

## Frequently asked questions

### Which is better, TPO or EPDM?
Neither is best everywhere. TPO is white and reflective with heat-welded seams, which suits hot climates and cooling-heavy buildings. EPDM is a durable rubber membrane with a long track record, popular in colder climates. Installation quality and the details at seams and edges matter as much as the membrane.

### How long does a flat roof last?
Single-ply and modified bitumen roofs commonly last about 15 to 30 years, depending on the product, thickness, installation, climate and maintenance.

### Is ponding water on a flat roof a problem?
Water that stands for more than about 48 hours after rain is generally a sign of a drainage or structural issue. It speeds up wear, can void some warranties and adds weight, so it's worth having a roofer look at it.

Commercial roofing

# Commercial roof coatings: restore or replace?
A coating can add years to a commercial roof for less than a replacement, but only if the roof underneath is in good shape.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: A roof coating (silicone, acrylic or polyurethane) can extend the life of a commercial roof that is still mostly dry and sound, usually for less than a full replacement and with less disruption. It's not a fix for a roof with widespread wet insulation, failing seams everywhere or structural problems. A roofer should check for trapped moisture before recommending one.

## When a coating can make sense

- The roof is aging but still watertight, with only isolated problems that can be repaired first.
- A moisture survey or core cuts show the insulation is mostly dry.
- You want a reflective surface to cut cooling loads.
- You want to delay a full tear-off for budget or tenant reasons.

## When replacement is the better call

- Large areas of wet insulation.
- Widespread seam failure, blistering or shrinkage.
- Deck damage or structural sagging.
- The roof already has the maximum number of layers allowed by code.

## Main coating types

- Silicone: handles ponding water and UV well. Recoating later usually requires silicone again.
- Acrylic: water-based, reflective and usually less expensive. Best where water drains well.
- Polyurethane and SPF: tough coatings, and spray polyurethane foam can add insulation and fix low spots.

## Questions to ask

- How did you check the roof for trapped moisture?
- What repairs will be made before coating, including seams, flashing and drains?
- What coating thickness will be applied, and how will you verify it?
- What warranty comes with the system, and what maintenance does it require?

Related: flat roof types compared and commercial roof maintenance checklist.

## Related guides
Flat roof types comparedCommercial roof maintenance checklistCommercial roofing: free inspections and quotesShould you repair or replace your roof?

## Frequently asked questions

### Can you put a coating on a leaking roof?
Coatings aren't a fix for an active leak or a wet roof. Leaks need to be repaired and wet insulation replaced first. A coating then goes over a sound, dry roof.

### Silicone or acrylic coating?
Silicone holds up well to ponding water and UV. Acrylic is usually less expensive and very reflective but is generally not recommended where water ponds. The existing roof type and local climate decide which is a better fit.

### Does a roof coating qualify as a new roof?
Usually not. It's a restoration that extends the life of the existing roof. Some coating systems come with their own manufacturer warranty, and the terms vary.

Commercial roofing

# Commercial roof maintenance checklist
Most commercial roof leaks start small. A simple routine catches them early and helps protect your warranty.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: Have a commercial roof inspected at least twice a year, typically in spring and fall, and after major storms. Keep drains and gutters clear, limit rooftop foot traffic, fix small seam and flashing problems quickly, and keep a log with photos. Many manufacturer warranties require documented maintenance.

## Twice-a-year checklist

- Clear drains, scuppers, gutters and downspouts of debris.
- Look for ponding water that stays more than about two days after rain.
- Check seams, edges and flashing at walls, curbs and penetrations.
- Look for blisters, cracks, punctures, shrinkage or loose fasteners.
- Check sealant at pitch pans, pipes and rooftop equipment.
- Inspect walkway pads around HVAC units and service areas.
- Look for interior signs: ceiling stains, wet insulation, musty smells.

## After a storm

- Check for blown-off edge metal, debris, punctures from hail or branches, and damaged rooftop units.
- Photograph damage with dates before any cleanup.
- Report damage to your insurer promptly. See filing a roof insurance claim.

## Keep a roof file
Keep the installation date, contractor, roof system and warranty, plus every inspection report, repair invoice and photo. It makes warranty claims, insurance claims and budgeting much easier.

## For HOAs and multifamily
Coordinate access with residents, plan work around weather and occupancy, and keep your reserve study up to date with current roof conditions.

Related: commercial roofing, flat roof types and roof coatings.

## Related guides
Commercial roofing: free inspections and quotesCommercial roof coatings: restore or replace?How to file a roof insurance claim, step by stepRoofing scams and red flags

## Frequently asked questions

### Who is responsible for the roof in a commercial lease?
It depends on the lease. Many leases make the landlord responsible for the roof structure and replacement, and some assign routine maintenance to the tenant. Check the lease before scheduling work.

### How should an HOA plan for roof replacement?
Many associations use a reserve study to estimate when roofs will need replacing and how much to set aside. Regular inspections help keep that estimate accurate and catch problems early.

Homeowner guide

# Metal roof vs. asphalt shingles: which is better?
The two most common choices for a new roof on a U.S. home, compared side by side.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: Asphalt shingles cost less up front and are what most U.S. homes have. Metal roofing usually costs more to install but lasts much longer, often 40 years or more versus roughly 15 to 30 for shingles, and it handles wind and wildfire embers well. If you plan to stay in the home a long time, metal can cost less over the roof's life. If you're selling in a few years or working to a tight budget, architectural shingles are usually the better value.

## Side-by-side

 | Asphalt shingles | Metal (standing seam or panels) | 

Up-front cost | Lowest of the common options | Higher, often much higher for standing seam | 

Typical lifespan | About 15–30 years | About 40–70 years | 

Wind | Good with high-wind rated shingles and proper nailing | Very good when installed to the panel's rating | 

Hail | Standard shingles bruise; Class 4 versions resist better | Resists punctures but can dent; dents may be cosmetic only | 

Fire | Most carry a Class A fire rating | Noncombustible; Class A assemblies common | 

Noise in rain | Quiet | Usually quiet over solid decking and underlayment | 

Repairs | Easy and cheap to patch | Needs a crew familiar with metal | 

## When shingles make more sense

- You expect to sell within about 10 years.
- Your budget is fixed and the roof needs replacing now.
- Your HOA limits roof materials or colors.

## When metal makes more sense

- You plan to stay 20+ years and want one roof for the long haul.
- You're in wildfire country or a high-wind coastal area.
- You get heavy snow and want it to shed easily (add snow guards over doors and walkways).

## Hail and insurance
In hail country, ask your insurer how they treat cosmetic dents on metal. Some policies exclude cosmetic damage to metal roofs, which can matter after a big storm. Class 4 impact-resistant shingles are the other option many hail-belt homeowners compare. See Class 4 shingles.

## Get both priced
Prices vary a lot by region and roof shape, so ask a roofer to quote both a shingle and a metal option on the same visit. Compare the full scope: tear-off, decking repair, underlayment, flashing, ventilation and warranty.

## Related guides
Roofing materials comparedHow long does a roof last?Are Class 4 impact-resistant shingles worth it?How much does a roof replacement cost?

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a metal roof louder than shingles?
Usually not by much. Over solid roof decking with underlayment, most homeowners say rain on a metal roof isn't noticeably louder. Metal over open framing, like on a barn, is louder.

### Does a metal roof attract lightning?
No. Metal doesn't make a strike more likely. If lightning does hit, metal is noncombustible and spreads the energy.

### Can metal go over existing shingles?
Sometimes, if local code allows it and the deck is sound. Many roofers still recommend a full tear-off so they can inspect and repair the decking.

### Which adds more resale value?
A newer roof of either kind helps a sale. Metal can be a selling point in some markets, but buyers rarely pay back the full extra cost.

Homeowner guide

# What happens during a roof inspection?
Know what a good inspection covers so you can tell a thorough roofer from a rushed sales pitch.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: A roof inspection usually takes 30 to 90 minutes for a typical house. A roofer checks the shingles or panels, flashing, vents, gutters, attic and signs of leaks, takes photos, and then tells you whether the roof needs a repair, a replacement or nothing yet. Ask for the photos and a written summary either way.

## What gets checked

- Roof covering: missing, cracked, curling or bruised shingles; granule loss; loose or dented metal panels.
- Flashing: around chimneys, skylights, walls and valleys, where most leaks start.
- Penetrations: pipe boots, vents and exhaust fans.
- Gutters and drainage: clogs, sagging and granules collecting in gutters.
- Attic (if accessible): daylight through boards, water stains, mold, ventilation and insulation.
- Decking: soft or spongy spots that suggest rot.

## What you should get afterward

- Photos of any damage, ideally with something for scale.
- A plain explanation: repair, replace, or monitor.
- A written quote that lists materials, scope, permit, cleanup and warranty if work is recommended.

## Questions to ask

- Can you show me the damage in the photos?
- Is this storm damage, age, or an installation problem?
- What happens if I wait a year?
- Is a repair realistic, or would you replace?

## Red flags
Be careful if someone damages the roof during the inspection, won't show you photos, or pushes you to sign a contract or insurance paperwork before you've had time to think. See roofing scams.

## When to get one
After a major hail or wind storm, before buying a home, when your roof is 15+ years old, or any time you see a leak or stain. Commercial roofs should be checked twice a year; see our commercial checklist.

## Related guides
9 signs you might need a new roofHow to tell if hail damaged your roofHow to choose a roofer you can trustRoofing scams and red flags

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a roof inspection free?
Many roofers offer free inspections when you're considering a repair or replacement. A home-sale inspection or a certified report for insurance may cost a fee.

### How long does a roof inspection take?
Often 30 to 90 minutes for a typical house. Larger or steeper roofs and attic checks take longer.

### Do I need to be home?
It helps, so the roofer can check the attic and show you photos, but many will inspect the outside without you there.

### Can a drone inspect my roof?
Yes, some roofers use drones for steep or fragile roofs. A drone can't check the attic or feel for soft decking, so it's not always a full substitute.

Homeowner guide

# Do you need a permit to replace your roof?
In most of the U.S., a full roof replacement needs a permit. Here's how it works and why it matters.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: Most cities and counties require a building permit for a full roof replacement, and many also require one for larger repairs. Small repairs like replacing a few shingles often don't need one. Rules are set locally, so check with your city or county building department. A licensed roofer usually pulls the permit and schedules the inspection for you.

## Why the permit matters

- An inspector checks the work against the building code, including underlayment, nailing, flashing and ventilation.
- Unpermitted work can cause trouble when you sell or when you file an insurance claim.
- Some insurers and lenders ask for proof of a permitted, inspected roof.
- In hurricane-prone areas, a permitted roof may help you qualify for wind-mitigation discounts.

## Who pulls it
Usually the roofing contractor. In many places only a licensed contractor (or the owner of a home they live in) can pull one. Be wary if a roofer asks you to pull the permit in your own name; that can make you responsible for code issues. Put "contractor obtains all permits" in the contract.

## What it costs
Permit fees vary widely by city and are often based on the job's value. Ask for the fee to be listed on your quote.

## Inspections
Some places inspect only at the end. Others also inspect mid-job, for example after the decking or underlayment goes on, especially in high-wind zones. Don't make final payment until the roof passes.

## HOAs
If you have an HOA, you may also need its approval for material and color, separate from the city permit.

## Related guides
How to choose a roofer you can trustHow much does a roof replacement cost?Roofing scams and red flagsWhat to expect during a roof replacement

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need a permit to repair my roof?
Small repairs often don't need one, but larger repairs or replacing a big section might. Your local building department sets the threshold.

### Can I get in trouble for an unpermitted roof?
You may be asked to get a permit after the fact, open up the work for inspection, or fix code issues, and it can complicate a home sale or insurance claim.

### How do I check if my roofer pulled a permit?
Many cities have online permit search by address. You can also ask the roofer for the permit number and call the building department.

### Does a roof-over (second layer) need a permit?
Usually yes, and some places don't allow more than two layers or ban overlays entirely.

Homeowner guide

# Roof warranties explained
Two different warranties cover a new roof. Here's what each one does and how to protect both.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: A new roof usually has two warranties. The manufacturer warranty covers defects in the shingles or other materials. The workmanship warranty comes from your roofer and covers installation mistakes, which cause most early roof problems. Get the workmanship warranty in writing, ask how many years it lasts, and keep your invoice and product details.

## Manufacturer warranty
Covers defective materials. Many shingle warranties are prorated after an initial period, so coverage shrinks over time. Some manufacturers offer enhanced warranties, which can include some labor coverage, when a roof is installed by a credentialed contractor using a full system of their components. Read what's actually covered; "lifetime" often has conditions.

## Workmanship warranty
Covers installation errors such as poor flashing, wrong nailing or bad ventilation. Length varies a lot between roofers. It's only worth something if the company is still in business, so ask how long they've operated locally.

## What can void a warranty

- Installing shingles in a way the manufacturer doesn't allow.
- Poor attic ventilation.
- Later work by another contractor on the same area.
- Not registering the warranty when registration is required.

## Questions to ask before signing

- How long is your workmanship warranty, and is it in the contract?
- Which manufacturer warranty will this roof get, and will you register it?
- Is the warranty transferable if I sell?
- What do I need to do to keep it valid?

## Related guides
How to choose a roofer you can trustRoofing materials comparedHow long does a roof last?What to expect during a roof replacement

## Frequently asked questions

### What does a lifetime roof warranty mean?
Usually that the manufacturer covers material defects for as long as you own the home, often prorated after the first years. It rarely covers labor or storm damage unless stated.

### Does a roof warranty cover storm damage?
Generally no. Storm damage is usually a homeowner's insurance matter. Some shingles have separate wind ratings or limited wind warranties.

### Is a roof warranty transferable?
Many manufacturer warranties can transfer once, sometimes with a notice or fee. Check the terms, as this can help when you sell.

### Who do I call with a warranty problem?
Start with your roofer for leaks or installation issues. For a suspected material defect, the manufacturer will usually want photos, the product details and proof of purchase.

Homeowner guide

# When is the best time of year to replace a roof?
Weather, demand and your region all affect when a roof replacement goes smoothest.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: Late spring through early fall is the most common roofing season in most of the U.S., with fall often the sweet spot: mild temperatures help shingles seal, and storms are less frequent in many areas. Roofers can install year-round in warm southern climates. If your roof is leaking or storm-damaged, don't wait for the "best" season; a temporary fix or replacement now usually costs less than water damage later.

## By season

- Spring: good weather in many places, but rain can cause delays and spring hail can create a backlog.
- Summer: long days and dry weather in much of the country; very high heat can make shingles easier to scuff and is hard on crews.
- Fall: often ideal. Moderate temperatures help self-sealing shingle strips bond before winter.
- Winter: possible in mild climates. In cold regions, crews may limit work, and shingles may need hand-sealing.

## By region

- Gulf and Atlantic coasts: try to finish before peak hurricane season (August to October).
- Hail belt (Texas to the Dakotas, Colorado): demand spikes after spring and summer hail; booking early helps.
- Northern states: fall is popular because of winter; book early.
- Desert Southwest: spring and fall avoid the hottest months.

## Scheduling tips

- Get quotes a month or two before you want the work.
- Ask about the roofer's backlog and weather-delay policy.
- Don't sign with a door-knocker just because a storm just passed. See roofing scams.

## Related guides
9 signs you might need a new roofWhat to expect during a roof replacementHow much does a roof replacement cost?What to do after storm damage

## Frequently asked questions

### Can a roof be replaced in winter?
Yes in many places. Roofers watch the temperature and may hand-seal shingles in cold weather. In snowy regions, winter jobs are less common.

### Is it cheaper to replace a roof in the off-season?
Sometimes. Some roofers have more scheduling flexibility in slower months, but material prices don't drop much by season.

### How far ahead should I book a roofer?
Several weeks is common, and longer after a big regional storm. Getting quotes early gives you time to compare.

### Should I wait to replace a leaking roof?
No. Get the leak stopped now, even with a temporary repair, to prevent damage inside the house.

Homeowner guide

# What to expect during a roof replacement
From the dumpster arriving to the final walkthrough, here's how a typical roof replacement goes.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: Most roof replacements on a typical single-family home take one to three days once work starts. The crew tears off the old roof, repairs damaged decking, installs underlayment, flashing and the new roof covering, then cleans up with magnets for nails. Larger, steeper or more complex roofs, and metal, tile or slate, can take longer.

## Before the job

- Sign a written contract with the scope, materials, price, payment schedule, permit and warranty.
- Confirm the permit and the start date.
- Move cars, patio furniture and grills away from the house.
- Take down wall hangings on top-floor walls; hammering can shake them.
- Cover items in the attic to catch dust.
- Plan for pets and kids; it's loud.

## Day by day

- Setup: dumpster or trailer, tarps over plants and siding.
- Tear-off: old shingles and underlayment come off down to the decking.
- Decking: rotted or soft boards are replaced. Contracts often price this per sheet, so ask in advance.
- Underlayment and ice/water shield in valleys, eaves and around penetrations, as code requires.
- Flashing, drip edge and vents.
- New roof covering.
- Ridge cap and final details.
- Cleanup: magnetic sweep for nails, debris hauled away.

## Final walkthrough
Walk the property with the crew lead. Ask for photos of the decking and underlayment stages, check gutters and the yard for nails, confirm the permit passed inspection, and get warranty paperwork before final payment. See roof warranties.

## Related guides
Do you need a permit to replace your roof?Roof warranties explainedHow to choose a roofer you can trustHow much does a roof replacement cost?

## Frequently asked questions

### How long does a roof replacement take?
One to three days of work is typical for an average single-family home with asphalt shingles. Weather, roof size, steepness and material can extend that.

### Do I need to be home during a roof replacement?
Not usually, but be reachable in case the crew finds rotten decking or needs a decision.

### What if they find rotten wood?
The roofer replaces damaged decking, usually at a price per sheet agreed in the contract. Ask to see photos.

### Will my gutters be removed?
Usually not, though some may be loosened to install drip edge. Ask whether gutter work is included.

Homeowner guide

# How to read and compare roofing estimates
Two quotes for the same roof can look very different. Here's how to compare them fairly.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: A good roofing estimate is written and itemized. It names the shingle or panel brand and product line, says whether the old roof is torn off, lists underlayment, ice and water shield, flashing, drip edge and ventilation, explains how rotten decking is priced, and includes the permit, cleanup, warranty and payment schedule. Compare quotes on the same scope, not just the bottom line.

## What should be on the estimate

- Company details: legal name, address, phone, and license number where your state licenses roofers.
- Roof size in squares (1 square = 100 sq ft) and the waste factor.
- Tear-off: how many layers are removed, and disposal.
- Decking: price per sheet for replacing rotten wood.
- Underlayment type, and ice and water shield locations.
- Flashing: new or reused at chimneys, walls and skylights.
- Ventilation: ridge vents, intake vents, any changes.
- Roof covering: brand, product line and color.
- Permit, cleanup, warranty and payment schedule.

## How to compare quotes fairly

- Put the quotes side by side and check each line above.
- Ask the lower bidder what's missing, and the higher bidder what's extra.
- Check that the same product line is quoted. "Architectural shingles" can mean very different products.
- Compare workmanship warranty length, not just the manufacturer's.

## Red flags

- A one-line quote ("new roof: $X") with no detail.
- A large cash deposit before materials arrive.
- Pressure to sign today or "this price expires tonight."
- An offer to cover or "waive" your insurance deductible, which is illegal in some states.

More: roof replacement cost and roofing scams.

## Related guides
How much does a roof replacement cost?How to choose a roofer you can trustRoofing scams and red flagsRoof warranties explained

## Frequently asked questions

### How many roofing quotes should I get?
For a full replacement, two or three written quotes is a common rule of thumb. For a small repair, one trusted roofer may be enough.

### Why are roofing quotes so different?
Different products, scope (tear-off, decking, flashing, ventilation), labor costs, overhead and warranty length. Line up the scope first.

### What is a roofing square?
A square is 100 square feet of roof surface. A roof is measured in squares, plus extra for waste on cuts, hips and valleys.

### How much deposit is normal for a roof?
It varies, and some states cap deposits on home improvement work. Be cautious about paying a large share before materials are delivered.

Homeowner guide

# Ice dams: what causes them and how to prevent them
If you see a thick ridge of ice and icicles at the edge of your roof, here's what's happening and what to do.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: Ice dams form when heat escaping from the house melts snow on the upper roof, and the meltwater refreezes at the colder roof edge. Water then backs up under the shingles and can leak into ceilings and walls. The long-term fix is to keep the roof deck cold with better attic air sealing, insulation and ventilation, plus ice and water shield along the eaves when the roof is replaced.

## Signs of an ice dam

- A thick ridge of ice along the eaves and heavy icicles.
- Water stains or dripping on ceilings or exterior walls during a thaw.
- Ice forming inside the soffits or gutters.

## What to do now (safely)

- Don't climb on an icy roof or chip at ice with tools. It's dangerous and damages shingles.
- A roof rake used from the ground can pull snow off the lower few feet of the roof.
- Professional ice dam removal with low-pressure steam is safer for the roof than hammers or chisels.
- Catch drips inside and photograph any damage for insurance.

## Long-term fixes

- Air-seal the attic floor: gaps around light fixtures, pipes and the attic hatch let warm air in.
- Add insulation to recommended levels for your climate.
- Balance ventilation with intake at the soffits and exhaust at the ridge.
- Ice and water shield at the eaves when you replace the roof; many cold-climate building codes require it.

Heat cables can help in trouble spots but don't fix the cause. More: roof leaking now?

## Related guides
Roof leaking? What to do right nowRoof and attic ventilation explained9 signs you might need a new roofHow to file a roof insurance claim, step by step

## Frequently asked questions

### Does homeowners insurance cover ice dam damage?
Many policies cover sudden water damage inside the home from an ice dam, but often not the ice removal itself or long-term maintenance problems. Check your policy and call your agent.

### Do gutters cause ice dams?
Not by themselves. Clogged gutters can make ice buildup worse, but the main cause is heat loss melting snow higher on the roof.

### Do heated roof cables work?
They can keep channels open in problem areas, but they use electricity and don't fix the heat loss behind the problem.

### Will a new roof stop ice dams?
A new roof with ice and water shield at the eaves limits leaks, but ice dams can still form unless attic insulation and ventilation are fixed.

Homeowner guide

# Roof and attic ventilation explained
Ventilation is easy to overlook, but it affects shingle life, ice dams, moisture and comfort.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: Most roofs over an attic need balanced ventilation: cool air comes in low at the soffits (intake) and warm, moist air leaves high at the ridge (exhaust). Poor ventilation can trap heat and moisture, shorten shingle life, cause mold and contribute to ice dams. Shingle manufacturers commonly require proper ventilation for full warranty coverage, so ask your roofer to check it during any replacement.

## Intake and exhaust

- Intake: soffit vents or edge vents near the eaves.
- Exhaust: ridge vents, box (static) vents, or powered fans near the top.
- Mixing different exhaust types on the same attic can short-circuit airflow; roofers usually pick one.

## Signs of poor ventilation

- Very hot attic in summer, high cooling bills.
- Frost or condensation on the underside of the roof deck in winter.
- Mold, musty smell or rusty nails in the attic.
- Ice dams in winter.
- Shingles aging faster on one section of roof.

## What to ask during a replacement

- Is my current ventilation adequate for the attic size?
- Are the soffit vents blocked by insulation?
- What exhaust will you install, and will it meet the shingle maker's requirements?

Note: some homes use an unvented ("conditioned") attic with insulation under the roof deck. That's a different design, so don't add vents without professional advice.

## Related guides
Ice dams: what causes them and how to prevent themHow long does a roof last?Roof warranties explainedWhat happens during a roof inspection?

## Frequently asked questions

### How much attic ventilation do I need?
A common rule in building codes is 1 square foot of net free vent area per 150 square feet of attic floor, or 1 per 300 in some cases with balanced intake and exhaust. Your roofer or local code will confirm.

### Are ridge vents better than box vents?
Ridge vents spread exhaust evenly along the peak and are common on new roofs. Box vents work too. The key is balance with intake at the eaves.

### Can too much ventilation be a problem?
Mixing exhaust types or having too little intake can pull air the wrong way, including weather. Balance matters more than quantity.

### Does ventilation affect my shingle warranty?
Often yes. Many shingle manufacturers require adequate ventilation for full warranty coverage.

# How to pay for a new roof: financing options
A new roof is a big expense. Here are the common ways homeowners pay for one, and what to watch out for.
Updated November 18, 2026 · By the Bedrock Roof team

 Quick answer: Homeowners usually pay for a new roof with savings, an insurance claim (if the damage is from a covered event like hail or wind), contractor-arranged financing, a personal loan, or a home equity loan or line of credit. Compare the total cost of borrowing, not just the monthly payment, and be careful with "0% interest" offers that charge deferred interest if not paid off in time.

## Common options

Option | Good for | Watch out for | 

Insurance claim | Sudden storm or hail damage | Deductible; age or wear isn't covered | 

Contractor financing | Convenience; promo rates | Deferred interest; fees; high rates after promo | 

Personal loan | No home collateral | Higher rates for weaker credit | 

Home equity loan / HELOC | Lower rates for homeowners with equity | Your home secures the loan; closing costs | 

Credit card | Small repairs | High interest if not paid quickly | 

## Assistance programs
Some homeowners qualify for help. Low-income and older homeowners can ask their local housing agency, Area Agency on Aging, or USDA Rural Development (for rural homes) about repair grants or loans. Some states also offer grants to strengthen roofs against hurricanes.

## Tips

- Get your quotes first, then compare financing separately.
- Read the fine print on any promotional rate.
- Never sign financing paperwork you don't understand on the spot.

More: does insurance cover roof replacement?

## Related guides
How much does a roof replacement cost?Does insurance cover roof replacement?How to read and compare roofing estimatesShould you repair or replace your roof?

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I finance a new roof with bad credit?
Possibly, through some contractor programs or lenders that work with lower credit scores, but expect higher rates. Compare total cost carefully.

### Is a home equity loan a good way to pay for a roof?
It often has lower rates than unsecured loans, but your home is collateral. It suits homeowners with equity and steady income.

### Are there grants for roof replacement?
Some local, state and federal programs help eligible homeowners, often based on income, age, disability or rural location. Availability varies by area.

### Does insurance pay for an old roof?
Insurance generally pays for sudden damage from covered events, not wear and age. Older roofs may be paid at actual cash value.
